refusal.message: Size 3 gives fewer rows than the 4 live participants, so a rank would get no row.

scatter.payloadSizeBasis: Java serialization size (java.io ObjectOutputStream, stream header included); not the RMI wire bytes; primitive parameters are sized as primitives, as RMI marshals them
scatter.latencyBasis: Measured on the root around the whole transfer: a fresh lookup of CollectiveEndpoint in the target node's RMI registry (including RMI's distributed garbage collection "dirty" call when this process holds no other live stub for that endpoint), then the method call with its arguments and reply over a real loopback socket. Experiment 1 shows the lookup and the call as separate figures; here they are one.

broadcast.payloadSizeBasis: Java serialization size (java.io ObjectOutputStream, stream header included); not the RMI wire bytes; primitive parameters are sized as primitives, as RMI marshals them
broadcast.latencyBasis: Measured on the root around the whole transfer: a fresh lookup of CollectiveEndpoint in the target node's RMI registry (including RMI's distributed garbage collection "dirty" call when this process holds no other live stub for that endpoint), then the method call with its arguments and reply over a real loopback socket. Experiment 1 shows the lookup and the call as separate figures; here they are one.

speedupBasis: All 4 nodes run inside one Java process on one machine, so they share its 16 available processors (as reported by the JVM; inside a container this can be lower than the machine's). The speedup cannot exceed 4, the smaller of the node count and that processor count, and other work on the machine lowers it further. For small matrices the scatter of A, the broadcast of B and the gather of C take longer than the multiply they split up, so the parallel run can be slower than the sequential one (a speedup below 1). Each node's compute time is measured on the node, around its multiply only; every other time is measured on the root. 1 untimed warm-up product was run first, so the JIT had compiled the multiply before the timed runs. The timed sequential product runs after 1 warm-up product and the timed parallel run after 2 full products (the warm-up and the sequential product), so the parallel run meets a slightly warmer JIT and processor cache than the sequential product did. Nothing else on the cluster is paused during a run: Experiment 1 calls, MPI collectives, Experiment 2 requests and other experiments can use the same nodes and processors at the same time, and any such work is included in these figures.
computeRoundTripBasis: Measured on the root around one remote compute call: a fresh lookup of MatrixEndpoint in the node's RMI registry (including RMI's distributed garbage collection "dirty" call when this process holds no other live stub for it), the call, the node's queue wait and multiply on its Experiment 2 executor, and the reply. The node's compute time, around the multiply only, is measured on the node.
gatherLatencyBasis: Measured on the root around one fetch of a block of C: a fresh lookup of MatrixEndpoint in the node's RMI registry (including RMI's distributed garbage collection "dirty" call when this process holds no other live stub for it), then the call and its reply over a real loopback socket.
